newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Afghan situation very tense -- Russia's Lebed.
newsitem.headline: Afghan situation very tense -- Russia's Lebed.

text.p: Russian national security supremo Alexander Lebed, in Brussels on a first-ever visit to the West, described the situation in Afghanistan on Sunday as very tense.

Lebed, a veteran of Moscow's ill-fated 10-year war in Afghanistan, said he saw a threat of military movements towards the borders of Tajikistan by the militant islamic Taleban militia which seized power in Kabul last week.
"(The situation is) very tense. Hostilities are continuing," he told reporters at Brussels airport, where he arrived on a visit to NATO headquarters.
"These military actions may have negative repercussions," President Boris Yeltsin's security adviser said.
Lebed, who rose to political prominence after winning strong support in this summer's presidential elections, spoke of militant notions of annexing parts of Tajikistan to Afghanistan.

He declined to say whether he would discuss the issue at talks on Monday with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana. But NATO officials have expressed concern that instability in Afghanistan could have consequences for member-nation Turkey.
Lebed's two-day NATO visit was scheduled to give him his first formal contact with the alliance that, for 20 years of his military career, he saw as his "imperialist" enemy.
Russia considers the former Soviet republics of Tajikistan and Uzbekistan to be part of its sphere of military and political influence.
These two Central Asian states and Turkmenistan share borders with Afghanistan.
Thousands of Russian soldiers are deployed on the Tajik frontier guarding against infiltration of Tajik radicals fighting a guerrilla war against the Moscow-backed government in Dushanbe.

The leaders of five former Soviet republics -- Russia, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan -- vowed at a summit in Almaty on Friday to defend areas bordering on Afghanistan, but said they would stop short of any intervention in the conflict.
Uzbek President Islam Karimov said Afghan warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek, was all that stood between the Taleban militia and the former Soviet republics.
But the Taleban has not so far moved against Dostum.

Lebed played the leading role in sealing a peace agreement with Islamic rebels in Russia's Chechen region on August 31, but he has been outspoken in his criticism of the Afghan Taleban since they swept into Kabul.

Lebed, scheduled to meet leaders of the 16-nation NATO alliance on Monday, said he intended to open a "complicated but civilised dialogue" over alliance plans to expand eastwards, incorporating countries of the former Soviet-led Warsaw Pact.
